chapters.title: The Song of Songs
chapters.html:
Song of Songs 1

1The Song of Songs, which is Solomon's.

2Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth!
For your love is better than wine;

3your oils are good for fragrance;
your name is oil poured out;
therefore the young women love you.

4Draw me after you; let us run.
The king has brought me into his chambers.
We will exult and rejoice in you;
we will praise your love more than wine.
Rightly do they love you.

5I am black and lovely,
daughters of Jerusalem,
like the tents of Kedar,
like the curtains of Solomon.

6Do not stare at me because I am dark,
because the sun has looked on me.
My mother's sons were angry with me;
they made me keeper of the vineyards;
my own vineyard I have not kept.

7Tell me, you whom my soul loves,
where you pasture your flock,
where you make it lie down at noon;
for why should I be like one who is veiled
beside the flocks of your companions?

8If you do not know,
most beautiful among women,
follow the tracks of the flock,
and pasture your young goats
beside the shepherds' tents.

9I compare you, my darling,
to a mare among Pharaoh's chariots.

10Your cheeks are lovely with ornaments,
your neck with strings of beads.

11We will make you ornaments of gold,
studded with silver.

12While the king was at his table,
my nard gave its fragrance.

13My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh
that lies all night between my breasts.

14My beloved is to me a cluster of henna blossoms
in the vineyards of En-gedi.

15How beautiful you are, my darling,
how beautiful!
Your eyes are doves.

16How handsome you are, my beloved,
how pleasant!
Our couch is green;

17the beams of our house are cedar;
our rafters are cypress.

Notes

  • v1 "The Song of Songs" — the Hebrew way of saying the greatest of songs, as "the holy of holies" is the most holy place and "vanity of vanities" (Ecclesiastes 1:2) is utter vanity. "Which is Solomon's" — lishlomoh, "of Solomon": by him, for him, or about him; the Hebrew allows all three.

  • v2 "Let him kiss me… your love is better than wine" — she turns from "him" to "you" within one line, from speaking of him to speaking to him. "Your love" — dodekha, love given and shown, caresses (the same word in 4:10). The Greek reads the same letters as dadayikh, "your breasts."

  • v3 "your name is oil poured out" — shem and shemen, the same play of sound as Ecclesiastes 7:1.

  • v5 "I am black and lovely" — shechorah, "black," darkened by the sun (v6). The Hebrew and the Greek join the two words with "and," not "but." "The tents of Kedar" — the black goat-hair tents of Kedar, a son of Ishmael (Genesis 25:13).

  • v6 "my own vineyard I have not kept" — her brothers set her to work in their vineyards, and she has had no care for her own. The vineyard stands for herself again in 8:12.

  • v7 "you whom my soul loves" — her name for him; it returns four times in 3:1–4. "Like one who is veiled" — ote'yah, a woman wrapped in a veil, as the Greek has it. A veiled woman wandering among shepherds' camps could be taken for a woman of another sort (compare Tamar, Genesis 38:14–15).

  • v9 "my darling" — ra'yati, from re'a, "companion, friend"; his name for her, nine times in the Song.

  • v14 "En-gedi" — the spring in the desert above the Dead Sea where David hid from Saul (1 Samuel 24:1).

  • vv15–16 "How beautiful you are… How handsome you are" — he speaks and she answers in his own words (hinnakh yafah… hinnekha yafeh).

chapters.title: The Winter Is Past
chapters.html:
Song of Songs 2

1I am a flower of Sharon,
a lily of the valleys.

2Like a lily among thorns,
so is my darling among the young women.

3Like an apple tree among the trees of the forest,
so is my beloved among the young men.
In his shade I delighted to sit,
and his fruit was sweet to my taste.

4He brought me to the house of wine,
and his banner over me was love.

5Sustain me with raisin cakes;
refresh me with apples,
for I am sick with love.

6His left hand is under my head,
and his right hand embraces me.

7I charge you, daughters of Jerusalem,
by the gazelles or by the does of the field,
that you not stir up or awaken love
until it pleases.

8The voice of my beloved!
He is coming,
leaping over the mountains,
bounding over the hills.

9My beloved is like a gazelle
or a young stag.
He stands behind our wall,
gazing through the windows,
peering through the lattice.

10My beloved spoke and said to me:
"Arise, my darling, my beautiful one,
and come away,

11for the winter is past;
the rain is over and gone.

12The flowers appear on the earth;
the time of singing has come,
and the voice of the turtledove
is heard in our land.

13The fig tree ripens its green figs,
and the vines in blossom give their fragrance.
Arise, my darling, my beautiful one,
and come away.

14My dove, in the clefts of the rock,
in the hiding place of the cliff,
let me see your face,
let me hear your voice,
for your voice is sweet,
and your face is lovely."

15Catch the foxes for us,
the little foxes
that spoil the vineyards,
for our vineyards are in blossom.

16My beloved is mine, and I am his;
he pastures among the lilies.

17Until the day breathes
and the shadows flee,
turn, my beloved, be like a gazelle
or a young stag
on the cleft mountains.

Notes

  • v1 "a flower of Sharon" — chavatselet, a meadow flower whose kind is not known for certain (crocus, asphodel and narcissus have all been proposed); the Greek has "a flower of the plain," and Sharon is the coastal plain. "Rose" in older English Bibles has nothing in the word to support it. "Lily" — shoshannah, a lily or a lotus.

  • v4 "his banner over me was love" — diglo, "his banner," the standard each tribe camped under (Numbers 2:2): his sign is raised over her for all to see. The Greek has "set love in order over me."

  • v7 "by the gazelles or by the does of the field" — bitsva'ot, "by the gazelles," is spelled exactly as tseva'ot, "hosts," and ayelot hassadeh, "does of the field," sounds like El Shaddai: the oath is sworn by wild creatures in words that echo the names of God. The Greek read them "by the powers and by the strengths of the field." The same charge comes again, word for word, in 3:5.

  • v7 "until it pleases" — love is not to be roused before its own time.

  • v12 "the time of singing" — zamir, "singing" or "pruning," both of them spring; the Greek has "pruning."

  • v16 "My beloved is mine, and I am his" — in 6:3 the order turns around, and in 7:10 it becomes "I am my beloved's, and his longing is for me."

  • v17 "the cleft mountains" — harei vater: "the mountains of Bether," a place not otherwise known, or "mountains of cutting." Bater is the word for the halves of the animals cut in two at the covenant with Abram (Genesis 15:10). The Greek has "mountains of hollows."

chapters.title: Him Whom My Soul Loves
chapters.html:
Song of Songs 3

1On my bed by night
I sought him whom my soul loves;
I sought him, but did not find him.

2I will rise now and go about the city,
in the streets and in the squares;
I will seek him whom my soul loves.
I sought him, but did not find him.

3The watchmen found me
as they went about the city.
"Have you seen him whom my soul loves?"

4Scarcely had I passed them
when I found him whom my soul loves.
I held him, and would not let him go
until I had brought him into my mother's house,
into the room of her who conceived me.

5I charge you, daughters of Jerusalem,
by the gazelles or by the does of the field,
that you not stir up or awaken love
until it pleases.

6Who is this coming up from the wilderness
like columns of smoke,
perfumed with myrrh and frankincense,
with all the powders of the merchant?

7It is Solomon's own litter,
with sixty mighty men around it,
of the mighty men of Israel,

8all of them holding swords,
trained in war,
each with his sword at his thigh
against the terror of the night.

9King Solomon made himself a carriage
from the wood of Lebanon.

10He made its posts of silver,
its back of gold,
its seat of purple;
its inside was inlaid with love
by the daughters of Jerusalem.

11Go out, daughters of Zion,
and look on King Solomon,
with the crown with which his mother crowned him
on the day of his wedding,
on the day of the gladness of his heart.

Notes

  • vv1–4 "him whom my soul loves" — four times in four verses, her name for him from 1:7. She seeks him in the night and the city, and the search ends only when she finds him.

  • v4 "into my mother's house" — as Isaac brought Rebekah into the tent of his mother Sarah (Genesis 24:67); again in 8:2.

  • v5 — the charge of 2:7, word for word.

  • v6 "Who is this" — zot is feminine: "who is she?", or "what is this?", the litter (feminine mittah) of v7. The same question opens 8:5.

  • v9 "a carriage" — appiryon, found only here; the Greek translator rendered it phoreion, "litter," a word it closely resembles.

  • v10 "inlaid with love" — ratsuf ahavah: its inside laid with love, the work or the gift of the daughters of Jerusalem; the Greek reads the same.

  • v11 "the crown with which his mother crowned him" — a wedding crown, not the crown of rule. This is the only wedding the Song names.

chapters.title: A Garden Locked
chapters.html:
Song of Songs 4

1How beautiful you are, my darling,
how beautiful!
Your eyes are doves
behind your veil.
Your hair is like a flock of goats
streaming down from Mount Gilead.

2Your teeth are like a flock of shorn ewes
that have come up from the washing,
all of them bearing twins,
and not one among them has lost its young.

3Your lips are like a scarlet thread,
and your mouth is lovely.
Your cheeks are like halves of a pomegranate
behind your veil.

4Your neck is like the tower of David,
built in rows of stone;
a thousand bucklers hang on it,
all of them shields of mighty men.

5Your two breasts are like two fawns,
twins of a gazelle,
that graze among the lilies.

6Until the day breathes
and the shadows flee,
I will go to the mountain of myrrh
and to the hill of frankincense.

7You are altogether beautiful, my darling;
there is no blemish in you.

8Come with me from Lebanon, my bride;
come with me from Lebanon.
Look down from the peak of Amana,
from the peak of Senir and Hermon,
from the dens of lions,
from the mountains of leopards.

9You have taken my heart, my sister, my bride;
you have taken my heart with one of your eyes,
with one jewel of your necklace.

10How beautiful is your love, my sister, my bride!
How much better is your love than wine,
and the fragrance of your oils than any spice!

11Your lips drip honey from the comb, my bride;
honey and milk are under your tongue;
the fragrance of your garments
is like the fragrance of Lebanon.

12A garden locked is my sister, my bride,
a spring locked, a fountain sealed.

13Your shoots are an orchard of pomegranates
with the choicest fruits,
henna with nard,

14nard and saffron,
calamus and cinnamon,
with every tree of frankincense,
myrrh and aloes,
with all the finest spices —

15a fountain of gardens,
a well of living water,
and streams flowing from Lebanon.

16Awake, north wind,
and come, south wind!
Blow on my garden;
let its spices flow.
Let my beloved come to his garden
and eat its choicest fruits.

Notes

  • v1 "How beautiful you are, my darling, how beautiful! Your eyes are doves" — the words of 1:15, now opening a description of her from her eyes downward; vv1–3 come back almost word for word in 6:5–7.

  • v2 "all of them bearing twins" — every tooth matched with its pair, and none missing.

  • v4 "built in rows of stone" — letalpiyyot, found only here, and its meaning is uncertain: built in courses of stone, or built "for weapons" or "for trophies." The Greek takes it as a place name, Thalpioth.

  • v7 "no blemish in you" — mum, the blemish that bars a priest from serving and an animal from the altar (Leviticus 21:17–23; 22:20–21).

  • v8 "my bride" — kallah, six times in 4:8–5:1 and nowhere else in the Song. "My sister" (v9) is a word of closeness for a wife, not a word of kinship.

  • v9 "You have taken my heart" — libbavtini, a verb made from lev, "heart"; the Greek has the same, "you have hearted me." "With one of your eyes" — a single glance was enough.

  • vv10–11 "How much better is your love than wine" — he gives back her own words of 1:2–3: dodim, "love," better than wine, and the fragrance of oils. "Honey and milk" — the land "flowing with milk and honey" (Exodus 3:8), with the order turned around.

  • v12 "A garden locked… a spring locked" — the second word is gal, "spring" (or "heap"), one letter from gan, "garden"; the Greek has "garden" both times.

  • v13 "an orchard" — pardes, a Persian word for a walled park (Nehemiah 2:8; Ecclesiastes 2:5). The Greek renders it paradeisos, its word for Eden's garden in Genesis 2:8, from which English has "paradise."

  • vv15–16 "a well of living water… Let my beloved come to his garden" — the words of Genesis 26:19, flowing water. In v16 she answers, and in one line "my garden" becomes "his garden."

chapters.title: This Is My Beloved
chapters.html:
Song of Songs 5

1I have come to my garden, my sister, my bride;
I have gathered my myrrh with my spice;
I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey;
I have drunk my wine with my milk.
Eat, friends; drink,
and be drunk, beloved ones!

2I was asleep, but my heart was awake.
The voice of my beloved, knocking:
"Open to me, my sister, my darling,
my dove, my perfect one,
for my head is wet with dew,
my locks with the drops of the night."

3I had taken off my robe;
how could I put it on?
I had washed my feet;
how could I soil them?

4My beloved put his hand in through the opening,
and my heart was stirred for him.

5I arose to open to my beloved,
and my hands dripped with myrrh,
my fingers with liquid myrrh,
on the handles of the bolt.

6I opened to my beloved,
but my beloved had turned and gone.
My soul went out when he spoke.
I sought him, but did not find him;
I called him, but he did not answer me.

7The watchmen found me
as they went about the city;
they struck me, they wounded me;
the watchmen of the walls
took my veil from me.

8I charge you, daughters of Jerusalem,
if you find my beloved,
what will you tell him?
That I am sick with love.

9What is your beloved more than another beloved,
most beautiful among women?
What is your beloved more than another beloved,
that you so charge us?

10My beloved is radiant and ruddy,
raised like a banner among ten thousand.

11His head is finest gold;
his locks are wavy,
black as a raven.

12His eyes are like doves
beside streams of water,
bathed in milk,
sitting by the full pools.

13His cheeks are like beds of spice,
towers of perfume.
His lips are lilies,
dripping liquid myrrh.

14His hands are rods of gold
set with stones of Tarshish;
his body is a plate of ivory
covered with sapphires.

15His legs are pillars of alabaster
set on bases of fine gold.
His appearance is like Lebanon,
choice as the cedars.

16His mouth is sweetness itself,
and he is altogether desirable.
This is my beloved, and this is my friend,
daughters of Jerusalem.

Notes

  • v1 "be drunk, beloved ones" — dodim, the word for "love" in 1:2 and 4:10, here most likely calling to the lovers themselves; it can also be read "be drunk with love." The Greek has "brothers." The garden of 4:12–16 is now entered: "my garden," "my myrrh," "my honey," eight times "my."

  • v2 "I was asleep, but my heart was awake" — the night scene of 3:1–4 again, but this time she hesitates (v3) and he is gone (v6). "My perfect one" — tammati, from tam, whole, without flaw; Job is tam (Job 1:1).

  • v4 "my heart was stirred for him" — literally "my inward parts murmured for him," me'ai hamu, the depths of a person moved, as in Isaiah 16:11 and Jeremiah 31:20.

  • v6 "My soul went out when he spoke" — bedabbero, "at his speaking": her life went out of her at his voice. The search of 3:1–2 begins again: "I sought him, but did not find him."

  • v7 "The watchmen found me as they went about the city" — the words of 3:3. Then she asked them; now they strike her.

  • v10 "raised like a banner" — dagul, from degel, "banner": the word of 2:4, "his banner over me was love." The Greek has "chosen out from ten thousands."

  • v12 "sitting by the full pools" — yoshevot al millet, "sitting on fullness": the doves sit by the brimming water, or the eyes sit full in their sockets like jewels in a setting (millu'at, the setting of the high priest's stones, Exodus 28:17).

  • v14 "stones of Tarshish… sapphires" — tarshish is one of the stones of the high priest's breastpiece (Exodus 28:20). Sappirim is the stone of the pavement under God's feet in Exodus 24:10, likely lapis lazuli, deep blue with flecks of gold.

  • v16 "this is my friend" — re'i, the man's form of ra'yati, "my darling," his name for her throughout. She gives it back to him.

speech.text: Song of Songs 5

I have come to my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my spice; I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk. Eat, friends; drink, and be drunk, beloved ones!

I was asleep, but my heart was awake. The voice of my beloved, knocking: "Open to me, my sister, my darling, my dove, my perfect one, for my head is wet with dew, my locks with the drops of the night."
I had taken off my robe; how could I put it on? I had washed my feet; how could I soil them?
My beloved put his hand in through the opening, and my heart was stirred for him.
I arose to open to my beloved, and my hands dripped with myrrh, my fingers with liquid myrrh, on the handles of the bolt.
I opened to my beloved, but my beloved had turned and gone. My soul went out when he spoke. I sought him, but did not find him; I called him, but he did not answer me.
The watchmen found me as they went about the city; they struck me, they wounded me; the watchmen of the walls took my veil from me.
I charge you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, what will you tell him? That I am sick with love.
What is your beloved more than another beloved, most beautiful among women? What is your beloved more than another beloved, that you so charge us?
My beloved is radiant and ruddy, raised like a banner among ten thousand.
His head is finest gold; his locks are wavy, black as a raven.
His eyes are like doves beside streams of water, bathed in milk, sitting by the full pools.
His cheeks are like beds of spice, towers of perfume. His lips are lilies, dripping liquid myrrh.
His hands are rods of gold set with stones of Tarshish; his body is a plate of ivory covered with sapphires.
His legs are pillars of alabaster set on bases of fine gold. His appearance is like Lebanon, choice as the cedars.
His mouth is sweetness itself, and he is altogether desirable. This is my beloved, and this is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem.

chapters.title: Return, Return, Shulammite
chapters.html:
Song of Songs 6

1Where has your beloved gone,
most beautiful among women?
Where has your beloved turned,
that we may seek him with you?

2My beloved has gone down to his garden,
to the beds of spice,
to pasture in the gardens
and to gather lilies.

3I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine;
he pastures among the lilies.

4You are beautiful, my darling, as Tirzah,
lovely as Jerusalem,
awesome as the bannered hosts.

5Turn your eyes away from me,
for they overwhelm me.
Your hair is like a flock of goats
streaming down from Gilead.

6Your teeth are like a flock of ewes
that have come up from the washing,
all of them bearing twins,
and not one among them has lost its young.

7Your cheeks are like halves of a pomegranate
behind your veil.

8There are sixty queens
and eighty secondary wives,
and young women without number.

9My dove, my perfect one, is the only one,
the only one of her mother,
the pure one of her who bore her.
The young women saw her and called her blessed;
the queens and secondary wives also, and they praised her:

10"Who is this who looks down like the dawn,
beautiful as the moon,
pure as the sun,
awesome as the bannered hosts?"

11I went down to the nut orchard
to look at the green shoots of the valley,
to see whether the vine had budded,
whether the pomegranates were in bloom.

12Before I knew it,
my soul had set me among the chariots
of my noble people.

13Return, return, Shulammite;
return, return, that we may look on you.
Why should you look on the Shulammite,
as on the dance of the two camps?

Notes

  • v3 "I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine" — the words of 2:16 with the order turned around: there she begins with him, here with herself.

  • v4 "as Tirzah… as Jerusalem" — Tirzah, the first royal city of the northern kingdom (1 Kings 14:17; 16:23), beside Jerusalem in the south; the name means "pleasing," and the Greek translates it so, "as good pleasure." "The bannered hosts" — nidgalot, "those under banners," troops ranked by their standards (Numbers 2:2), and the Greek has "ranks set in order"; beside the dawn, moon and sun of v10 they may also be the hosts of the sky.

  • vv5–7 — the praise of 4:1–3 comes back nearly word for word: here "from Gilead" for "from Mount Gilead," "ewes" for "shorn ewes," and the lips and mouth of 4:3 are left out.

  • v8 "secondary wives" — pilagshim, the word rendered so throughout these books.

  • vv9–10 "the pure one… pure as the sun" — barah both times: she is pure to her mother, and pure as the sun. "The moon… the sun" — levanah, "the white one," and chammah, "the hot one," words of poetry, not the common names.

  • v12 — the Hebrew is one of the hardest lines in the book: lo yada'ti nafshi samatni markevot ammi nadiv, "I did not know; my soul set me (on) the chariots of my people, a noble." Ammi nadiv may also be a name, Amminadib, as the Greek takes it (Aminadab).

  • v13 "Shulammite" — hashulammit, with the article: a title more than a name. Its letters are those of Shelomoh, Solomon, and of shalom; the Greek has "the Shunammite," as of Abishag the Shunammite (1 Kings 1:3). This verse is the first of chapter 7 in the Hebrew; the English numbering is followed. "The two camps" — hammachanayim, the name Jacob gave the place where God's messengers met him (Genesis 32:2).

speech.text: Song of Songs 6
Where has your beloved gone, most beautiful among women? Where has your beloved turned, that we may seek him with you?
My beloved has gone down to his garden, to the beds of spice, to pasture in the gardens and to gather lilies.
I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine; he pastures among the lilies.
You are beautiful, my darling, as Tirzah, lovely as Jerusalem, awesome as the bannered hosts.
Turn your eyes away from me, for they overwhelm me. Your hair is like a flock of goats streaming down from Gilead.
Your teeth are like a flock of ewes that have come up from the washing, all of them bearing twins, and not one among them has lost its young.
Your cheeks are like halves of a pomegranate behind your veil.
There are sixty queens and eighty secondary wives, and young women without number.

My dove, my perfect one, is the only one, the only one of her mother, the pure one of her who bore her. The young women saw her and called her blessed; the queens and secondary wives also, and they praised her:
"Who is this who looks down like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, pure as the sun, awesome as the bannered hosts?"
I went down to the nut orchard to look at the green shoots of the valley, to see whether the vine had budded, whether the pomegranates were in bloom.
Before I knew it, my soul had set me among the chariots of my noble people.
Return, return, Shulammite; return, return, that we may look on you. Why should you look on the Shulammite, as on the dance of the two camps?

chapters.title: His Longing Is for Me
chapters.html:
Song of Songs 7

1How beautiful are your feet in sandals,
noble daughter!
The curves of your thighs are like jewels,
the work of a craftsman's hands.

2Your navel is a rounded bowl;
may it never lack mixed wine.
Your belly is a heap of wheat,
fenced in with lilies.

3Your two breasts are like two fawns,
twins of a gazelle.

4Your neck is like an ivory tower.
Your eyes are pools in Heshbon,
by the gate of Bath-rabbim.
Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon,
looking toward Damascus.

5Your head crowns you like Carmel,
and the flowing hair of your head is like purple;
a king is held captive in its tresses.

6How beautiful you are, and how pleasant,
love, among delights!

7Your stature is like a palm tree,
and your breasts are like its clusters.

8I said, "I will climb the palm tree
and take hold of its fruit."
Let your breasts be like clusters of the vine,
and the fragrance of your breath like apples,

9and your mouth like the best wine,
going down smoothly for my beloved,
gliding over the lips of sleepers.

10I am my beloved's,
and his longing is for me.

11Come, my beloved, let us go out into the field;
let us lodge in the villages;

12let us go early to the vineyards
and see whether the vine has budded,
whether its blossoms have opened,
whether the pomegranates are in bloom.
There I will give you my love.

13The mandrakes give their fragrance,
and at our doors are all choice fruits,
new as well as old,
which I have stored up for you, my beloved.

Notes

  • v1 "noble daughter" — bat nadiv, "daughter of a noble," a title of honor; the Greek takes it as a name, "daughter of Nadab." The Hebrew numbers this verse 7:2, since its 7:1 is English 6:13; the English numbering is followed.

  • vv1–5 — the praise now runs from her feet upward, the reverse of 4:1–5. v3 repeats 4:5 without its last line.

  • v4 "the gate of Bath-rabbim" — a gate of Heshbon, the name meaning "daughter of many." Heshbon was the city of Sihon east of the Jordan (Numbers 21:25–26).

  • v5 "a king is held captive in its tresses" — rehatim, "tresses," is the word for the troughs where Jacob's flocks came to drink (Genesis 30:38, 41): her hair flows like water in channels, and the king is caught in it.

  • v9 "going down smoothly for my beloved" — in the middle of the line his praise becomes her answer: "for my beloved." "Smoothly" — lemeisharim, the word of 1:4, "rightly." "The lips of sleepers" — the Greek reads "my lips and teeth."

  • v10 "his longing is for me" — teshuqah, found only here and in Genesis 3:16 ("Toward your man shall be your longing, and he shall rule over you") and 4:7. Here the longing runs the other way, from the man to the woman, and nothing is said of rule. The words of 2:16 and 6:3 come a third time, changed.

  • v11 "in the villages" — bakkefarim, "villages," or "among the henna bushes," the plant of 1:14 and 4:13 (kofer, plural kefarim).

  • v13 "The mandrakes" — duda'im, the plant Leah and Rachel bargained over, believed to help a woman conceive (Genesis 30:14–16). The word sounds like dodai, "my love," in v12, and dodi, "my beloved," at the end of this verse.

chapters.title: Love Is Strong as Death
chapters.html:
Song of Songs 8

1If only you were like a brother to me,
who nursed at my mother's breasts!
If I found you outside, I would kiss you,
and no one would despise me.

2I would lead you and bring you
into my mother's house;
she would teach me.
I would give you spiced wine to drink,
the juice of my pomegranate.

3His left hand is under my head,
and his right hand embraces me.

4I charge you, daughters of Jerusalem:
why should you stir up or awaken love
until it pleases?

5Who is this coming up from the wilderness,
leaning on her beloved?
Under the apple tree I awakened you;
there your mother was in labor with you;
there she who bore you was in labor.

6Set me as a seal upon your heart,
as a seal upon your arm,
for love is strong as death,
jealousy is fierce as Sheol.
Its flashes are flashes of fire,
the flame of Yah.

7Many waters cannot quench love,
nor can rivers sweep it away.
If a man gave all the wealth of his house for love,
he would be utterly scorned.

8We have a little sister,
and she has no breasts.
What shall we do for our sister
on the day when she is spoken for?

9If she is a wall,
we will build on her a battlement of silver;
but if she is a door,
we will enclose her with boards of cedar.

10I am a wall,
and my breasts are like towers;
then I was in his eyes
as one who finds peace.

11Solomon had a vineyard at Baal-hamon;
he gave the vineyard to keepers;
each was to bring for its fruit
a thousand pieces of silver.

12My own vineyard is before me.
The thousand are yours, Solomon,
and two hundred for those who keep its fruit.

13You who dwell in the gardens,
companions are listening for your voice;
let me hear it.

14Flee, my beloved,
and be like a gazelle
or a young stag
on the mountains of spices.

Notes

  • v2 "she would teach me" — telammedeni, "she would teach me," that is, her mother, or "you would teach me"; the Hebrew form allows both. The Greek has instead "into the room of her who conceived me," as in 3:4.

  • v4 — the charge of 2:7 and 3:5, but without the gazelles and does, and with mah, "why," for im: not "that you not," but "why should you?" The Greek gives the full form of 2:7.

  • v5 "Who is this coming up from the wilderness" — the question of 3:6, now answered by the two of them coming together. "Under the apple tree" — the tree of 2:3, where she sat in his shade.

  • v6 "Set me as a seal" — a seal was worn on a cord over the heart or as a ring on the hand (Genesis 38:18; Jeremiah 22:24), the mark of its owner. "Jealousy" — qin'ah, the zeal that will not share what is its own; from the same root God calls Himself "a jealous God" (Exodus 20:5). "The flame of Yah" — shalhevetyah: "the flame of Yah," the short form of God's name (as in Hallelujah), or "a mighty flame," with -yah making the word a superlative. If the first, it is the only place God is named in the Song. The Greek has "its flames."

  • v7 "he would be utterly scorned" — boz yavuzu lo, the verb doubled for force: love cannot be bought.

  • vv8–10 — the brothers of 1:6 speak of their young sister: a wall to be defended, a door to be guarded. She answers that she is a wall, and in his eyes she has found shalom, peace, the word inside the names Shulammite and Solomon (6:13).

  • vv11–12 "My own vineyard is before me" — karmi shelli, the words of 1:6, "my own vineyard I have not kept." Solomon may have his vineyard worked by keepers for a thousand pieces of silver; hers is her own to give.

  • v14 "Flee, my beloved, and be like a gazelle" — berach, "flee" or "run" (the Greek has "flee"); the last line answers 2:17, "turn, my beloved, be like a gazelle," but where those mountains were cleft, these are "mountains of spices," like "the mountain of myrrh" of 4:6.
